transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Sam Patel (Redwood AE), Lara Kim (Redwood SE), Mike Chen (TideWave CTO), Priya Anand (TideWave ML Engineer), Rajiv Menon (TideWave Infra)

[00:00] Sam Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, mic check, i'm sam from redwood, with me is lara from the se team. how's everyth — how's everyone doing
[00:12] Mike Chen: good thanks, busy week but ready to dig in. we wanted to make sure we cover both latency SLOs and throughput for streaming agent workloads, plus security basics.
[00:26] Lara Kim: great, quick agenda: 1) current stack and traffic shape, 2) p95 targets and concurrency, 3) streaming specifics and token/sec expectations, 4) deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private) and tradeoffs. any additions?
[00:40] Priya Anand: if possible please talk about prefix caching and how it affects streaming, we've run into weird stalls when KV-cache cold starts happen.
[00:50] Sam Patel: yep we'll cover that. quick qual: what models are you running today and what's the backend — are you on openai, self-hosted, hybrid?
[01:05] Mike Chen: mainly OpenAI for now, few experiments on Cohere. we're evaluating moving heavy traffic to dedicated infra to cut costs and control privacy. we also have an internal small LLM for embeddings.
[01:20] Rajiv Menon: infra note — we run on gcp us-west, our burst windows are usually 9am-6pm PT, roughly 300 concurrent requests at peak, with spikes to 450 for 5-10 minutes.
[01:36] Lara Kim: ok that's helpful. when you say 300 concurrent requests, is that concurrent user sessions or concurrent generation streams?
[01:44] Rajiv Menon: generation streams — multiple streaming tokens per session, average sequence 512 tokens, some up to 4k.
[01:52] Priya Anand: and our target p95 for interactive agent flows is ~200ms end-to-end, server-to-client for streaming initial chunk ideally <120ms but we can accept 250ms for full response in non-streaming use-cases.
[02:10] Sam Patel: good, so two SLOs: streaming initial chunk p95 <=120ms and non-streaming completion p95 <=200-250ms. noted. what are your token/sec goals?
[02:20] Priya Anand: we want to sustain ~2.5k tokens/sec average, peak 8k tokens/sec for short windows.
[02:30] Lara Kim: that lines up with what we've seen for similar customers. quick callout: tokens/sec depends a lot on model size, sequence length, and whether KV cache hits. we'll propose bench configs that mirror your 512/4k distribution.
[02:46] Mike Chen: how does redwood handle continuous batching and streaming latency; doesn't batching add latency? i'm worried about tail latencies for p95.
[02:57] Lara Kim: great question. our runtime uses adaptive batching that prioritizes latency SLOs — if a request needs streaming, it gets prioritized into smaller micro-batches and we favor immediate first-chunk generation while heavier throughput jobs are batched more aggressively. so batching reduces cost without blowing p95. there are knobs to set max batching delay.
[03:18] Mike Chen: ok and prefix caching? we've seen big wins when the first 128 tokens are cached across calls, but cold start kills us.
[03:27] Lara Kim: we support KV-prefix caching and configurable TTLs. in Dedicated/Private you can pin hot prefixes in memory across instances; hosted also supports caching tiers but depending on tenant isolation there may be limits. cold starts are mitigated with warm pools and pre-warming — we can include that in the PoC.
[03:42] Priya Anand: any differences in quantization or performance between hosted and private? also heard of mismatched kernels with quantized models.
[03:52] Lara Kim: kernel selection and quantization paths are consistent across deployments but private may allow you to use custom kernels or nonstandard quantization profiles for extra density. hosted uses tested quant profiles to ensure determinism and metrics. sometimes quantization increases per-token throughput but may slightly change latency distribution — we'll show numbers in the benchmark.
[04:11] Rajiv Menon: security stuff — we require encrypt-at-rest via our KMS, SSO (SAML), and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. private would be ideal but hosted could work if data never leaves VPC. can you integrate with our on-prem KMS?
[04:25] Sam Patel: yes, for Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; Dedicated can integrate with KMS via VPC peering and HSM connectors depending on topology. we'll send the network architecture guide.
[04:37] Mike Chen: competitive check — why choose redwood over openai/dedicated enterprise or self-hosting?
[04:45] Sam Patel: two things: predictable unit economics and operational tooling for rolling models and observability. we surface token-level cost, per-route latency, and have fallbacks so your app doesn't blow up on capacity events — plus consistent API across Hosted/Dedicated/Private so you can move workloads.
[05:02] Priya Anand: can you talk about streaming metrics instrumentation? we need per-chunk latency and token emission rates to debug stalls.
[05:11] Lara Kim: yes, console exposes per-request traces including first-chunk time, per-token spacing, and KV hit rates. we can add custom traces to emit metrics to your prometheus via exporter in Private.
[05:25] Mike Chen: ok let's talk about benchmarking — what will you run and what do you need from us?
[05:31] Lara Kim: we'll run two passes: 1) a latency-focused pass with small batch sizes and streaming enabled to validate p95 initial-chunk numbers, 2) a throughput pass that ramps concurrent streams to measure sustained tokens/sec and peak bursts. we'll need your prompt set, expected token distributions, and a sample of user concurrency shapes.
[05:50] Priya Anand: we can provide a 2000-prompt set and synthetic load generator; prefer the test to simulate 30 second conversations with intermittent think-times.
[05:58] Sam Patel: perfect. we'll also include prefix-cache warm/cold scenarios. for numbers, for example, a 13B quantized model on Dedicated 4xA100 typically yields ~6-8k tokens/sec sustained with good KV hit rates; 70B family will be lower per GPU but higher quality.
[06:18] Mike Chen: got it. what about cost tradeoffs — quantized dedicated vs hosted?
[06:24] Sam Patel: hosted is convenience-first with usage pricing; dedicated is commit-based and cheaper at scale, private has platform fee plus infra. we'll send a comparative cost worksheet tailored to your traffic.
[06:35] Rajiv Menon: what about autoscaling latency during spikes? we can't accept long warm times for new nodes.
[06:42] Lara Kim: Dedicated supports warm pools and pre-baked images; autoscaling can be based on request queue length and can spin up burst nodes with prefetched weights. startup time for a warmed image is low — a couple seconds if model already loaded elsewhere in the pool. for private you'll control images and can pre-warm too.
[06:59] Mike Chen: okay interesting. any recommended p95 targets for agent-like streaming? your earlier comment of <120ms first-chunk — is that realistic at our concurrency?
[07:08] Lara Kim: depends on sequence length and model; with 512 avg and micro-batching we can hit ~80-120ms first-chunk p95 on Dedicated for 300 concurrent streams if KV hit rate is high. if KV misses, p95 can move up 2-3x. we'll quantify in the bench.
[07:27] Priya Anand: can you explain how token/sec is measured — do you count emitted tokens only or compute tokens? we do both in our metrics.
[07:35] Sam Patel: we report emitted tokens/sec end-to-end and server-token throughput. in the benchmark we will provide both columns.
[07:42] Mike Chen: what about streaming backpressure if client disconnects mid-stream? we need predictable resource reclamation.
[07:50] Lara Kim: runtime tracks per-request memory and KV usage and enforces timeouts; if a client disconnects we free KV cache references after a short grace period. there are also per-tenant quotas to prevent noisy neighbors.
[07:59] Rajiv Menon: curious about the 'fallback' behavior you mentioned — if primary model reaches capacity do you route to a cheaper model?
[08:06] Sam Patel: yes we support auto-fallback policies: route-to-cheaper quantized variant, or to a smaller model population, or to a degraded 'fast' path that returns shorter responses. all policy-driven and configurable.
[08:19] Priya Anand: in practical terms, if we need p95<250ms for completions, do you recommend Dedicated or Private?
[08:26] Lara Kim: Dedicated gives you SLA-backed capacity and predictable latency costs; Private gets you more control over network and compliance but may require your infra team to tune perf. for fastest onboarding, start with Dedicated for the PoC, then consider Private if you need on-prem KMS or air-gapped compliance.
[08:43] Mike Chen: ok that's helpful. let's talk test matrix — for the throughput run, do you test sustained 30-minute windows or shorter bursts?
[08:51] Lara Kim: we'll do both: 30-minute sustained run for steady-state tokens/sec and 10-minute burst ramps to measure autoscale and tail SLOs.
[08:58] Priya Anand: include worst-case sequences (4k tokens) because our agents sometimes have long context chains.
[09:05] Sam Patel: noted. we'll simulate 90% 512-token and 10% 4k to match your mix.
[09:12] Mike Chen: any pitfalls you've seen customers hit in production around streaming and batching?
[09:18] Lara Kim: common issues: 1) not warming prefixes which kills p95 on cold starts, 2) client-side buffering causing perceived stutter, 3) improper quotas that allow noisy jobs to starve interactive flows. instruments and alerts help.
[09:33] Mike Chen: bummer, we did see buffering on our websockets layer.
[09:37] Priya Anand: quick question: are there recommended gRPC vs HTTP streaming differences? we use websockets to client.
[09:44] Lara Kim: we support multiple streaming transports; gRPC has slightly lower overhead per-chunk but websockets are fine if you handle small chunk sizes and backpressure. we'll include guidance in the network doc.
[09:56] Sam Patel: switching gears — let's define acceptance criteria for the PoC. what would success look like for TideWave?
[10:02] Mike Chen: 1) meet p95 first-chunk <=120ms for 90% of interactive sample, 2) sustain 2.5k tokens/sec for 30m with <5% dropped requests, 3) KV caching reduces average latency by at least 30% on hot paths, 4) security checklist passed (KMS, SSO, logs).
[10:20] Priya Anand: plus cost model that shows 30-40% savings vs current openai spend at our projected scale.
[10:28] Sam Patel: good set. we'll map that into the PoC success matrix.
[10:34] Mike Chen: someone mentioned 'allocation tiers' — can we reserve headroom for spikes?
[10:38] Lara Kim: yes, Dedicated has reservation and burst pools you can buy; private you can size as you like. reservation reduces need for warm-up and ensures capacity under SLA.
[10:47] Rajiv Menon: about observability — will we get exportable traces? we need to onboard our ops.
[10:53] Sam Patel: yes, the console supports trace export and alerts; we'll also enable a prometheus exporter for request-level metrics in Private.
[11:02] [~11:02 - interruption/static] (unidentified voice): sorry dropped a sec, rejoin —
[11:08] Mike Chen: no problem.
[11:12] Lara Kim: quick note on kernel selection: models compiled for specific GPU architectures can change perf curves; we'll pick kernels based on your target hardware in the bench — if you're on A100 vs H100 numbers differ.
[11:27] Rajiv Menon: we're on A100 now but evaluating H100 for next quarter.
[11:31] Sam Patel: perfect, we'll run bench on A100 images and extrapolate H100 numbers.
[11:36] Priya Anand: any example numbers you can share offhand? even rough order of magnitude helps for planning.
[11:43] Lara Kim: rough: a quantized 13B on 4xA100 dedicated pool ~6-8k tokens/sec sustained; 70B on 8xA100 may be 3-4k tokens/sec per GPU set depending on quant; H100 often gives 1.5-2x improvement on certain kernels. these are ballpark; bench will be authoritative.
[12:05] Mike Chen: will you run both streaming and non-streaming payloads?
[12:09] Lara Kim: yes, separate runs. streaming profile focuses on latency-first, throughput profile disables micro-batching to push tokens/sec.
[12:18] Sam Patel: we'll share the benchmark script repo and instructions; you'll be able to rerun in your env for Private.
[12:26] Priya Anand: question on tokenization consistency — we count tokens differently from openai sometimes; how do you normalize?
[12:33] Lara Kim: bench will run tokenization using same tokenizer as model; we'll provide both model-token counts and 'customer-token' counts if you use a different tokenizer.
[12:41] Mike Chen: about pricing again — can you give an example pricing scenario for our expected monthly tokens?
[12:48] Sam Patel: we'll send a pricing worksheet with Hosted per-token, Dedicated commit scenarios and an example amortized infra cost for Private. also include network egress numbers.
[12:59] Priya Anand: also include cost of warm pools vs on-demand. that's a big factor.
[13:04] Lara Kim: noted.
[13:06] Mike Chen: any regulatory constraints we should be aware of for private deployments? data residency etc.
[13:12] Sam Patel: private supports region pinning and on-prem; we'll surface compliance docs and the list of data residency capabilities.
[13:19] Rajiv Menon: back to streaming — do you measure per-token spacing jitter? we need that to debug client stalls.
[13:26] Lara Kim: yes, the trace includes per-token emit timing and jitter metrics; we'll show example dashboards.
[13:33] Priya Anand: okay i think our required artifacts are: 1) bench results, 2) pricing sheet, 3) security docs and network guide, 4) PoC plan and success criteria.
[13:45] Sam Patel: that's a clean action list, we'll own those.
[13:49] Mike Chen: timeline — when can the bench run start?
[13:53] Sam Patel: if you can share the prompt set and concurrency profile by Friday (2025-04-04) we can kick bench early next week and share initial results within 3 business days.
[14:03] Priya Anand: we can do that.
[14:05] Rajiv Menon: one more technical nuance — how are KV cache evictions handled under pressure? we need eviction policies configured for multi-tenant environment.
[14:15] Lara Kim: eviction policies are pluggable: LRU-like by default, with TTLs and weightings; in Dedicated you can reserve memory per-tenant to reduce evictions. we'll include config examples.
[14:28] Mike Chen: ok. last question from my side — if during PoC you hit a regression vs openai quality, how do you handle rollback?
[14:36] Sam Patel: we version models and support safe rollback plus A/B rollouts; canary traffic percentages are configurable and we run evals on your prompt set to track regressions. quality alerts can halt rollouts automatically.
[14:48] Priya Anand: sweet.
[14:51] [14:51 - background chatter]
[15:00] Sam Patel: quick recap of next steps then: sam will send pricing and security docs, lara will set up the bench harness and run initial tests, tidewave to provide prompt set and concurrency profiles — target deliverables next week.
[15:15] Mike Chen: yep that works. any blockers we should flag?
[15:19] Rajiv Menon: none on our side; just need the bench scripts to not assume weird envs.
[15:24] Sam Patel: we'll make them reproducible.
[15:28] Priya Anand: thanks, this was productive.
[15:31] Lara Kim: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the PoC kickoff.
[15:35] Mike Chen: thanks all.

End of meeting.
Notes on transcript: auto-transcription had a few mis-heard terms ("K V cash" instead of KV cache, "quanti zation" separator) and minor timestamp jitter.
